description: Full-length 53-question simulation in the applied-scenario style (120 minutes): constraint-driven scenarios, code and config snippets, and short options that are all real features but only one fits.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A report generator calls the first-party API with `stop_sequences=["###SUMMARY", "###DETAILS"]` and splits the output into sections. A response arrives with `stop_reason` set to `stop_sequence`. The code must know which marker ended the text so it can open the matching section. Where should it read that?

options.text: The `stop_details` object on the response, which names the matched marker
Read `response.stop_sequence`, which holds the exact string that matched
The tail of the last `text` block, searched for either marker string
Run the request once per marker and see which single call stops early

questions.explanation: When generation ends on a custom stop sequence, `stop_reason` is `stop_sequence` and the response's `stop_sequence` field carries the string that matched. Branching on that field is simpler and safer than scanning the output text, and it works however many sequences are configured.

distractor_explanations.A: `stop_details` explains refusals and is `null` for every other stop reason, so it never names a stop sequence.
distractor_explanations.C: Scanning text is fragile and unnecessary. The API returns the matched string in a dedicated field.
distractor_explanations.D: That multiplies cost and latency. The response already reports which configured string was matched.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A summarizer on a Sonnet 4.5 or newer model sets `max_tokens=32000` on every call so it never has to estimate input size. Inputs run from 20k to 190k tokens. For the largest ones the call returns HTTP 200 with `stop_reason` set to `model_context_window_exceeded`, and the text so far reads coherently. How should the service treat this response?

options.text: As a `max_tokens` stop, so raise the limit and retry for the missing text
As a missing opt-in, so add the `model-context-window-exceeded-2025-08-26` beta header
As a malformed request, so shorten the input and send the call again
As valid but cut short by the context window; use the text and flag it as truncated

questions.explanation: On Sonnet 4.5 and newer models, `model_context_window_exceeded` is an ordinary stop reason on a 200 response. It means generation ran until the model's absolute context window was full, which happened before `max_tokens`. The output is valid but incomplete. Analogy: a notebook with a fixed number of pages. You asked for a 32-page chapter, but only 10 pages were left, so the writer stopped at the last page. The writing is real, just unfinished, and the page limit is a different thing from the chapter length you requested. A beta header would only matter on older models, and an invalid-request error would mean the notebook was refused before any writing began.

distractor_explanations.A: `max_tokens` is a separate stop reason for your own cap. This response stopped earlier, at the model's absolute window.
distractor_explanations.B: That header is only for models older than Sonnet 4.5. It surfaces the reason and does not enlarge the window.
distractor_explanations.C: An input that cannot fit fails validation before generation starts. Here generation ran and then hit the window, so a response exists.

questions.prompt:
An agent loop answers tool calls like this:

```python
results = [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": b.id, "content": run(b)}
           for b in resp.content if b.type == "tool_use"]
results.append({"type": "text", "text": "Here are the results."})
messages += [{"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content},
             {"role": "user", "content": results}]
resp = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=1024,
                              tools=TOOLS, messages=messages)
```

Now and then the final call returns a few tokens, empty `content`, and `stop_reason` of `end_turn`. Which change addresses the cause?

options.text: Drop the trailing `text` block so the user turn has only `tool_result` blocks
Resend the identical request until the reply contains text
Raise `max_tokens` so the reply has room to finish after the tool results
Add a system prompt line telling Claude to always write a closing answer after tools

questions.explanation: Claude sometimes returns an empty `end_turn` response when a text block sits right after the `tool_result` blocks, because it learns to expect fresh user input at that point and ends its turn. The fix is to send tool results on their own. If a response is still empty, add a continuation prompt in a new user message. Analogy: a barista who receives the order slip with a note stapled on saying "that's all, thanks!" will assume the order is finished and walk away. Hand over the slip alone. A larger token budget does not help, because the turn ended on purpose.

distractor_explanations.B: The documented advice is not to simply retry, since Claude has already decided its turn is over.
distractor_explanations.C: A few tokens with `end_turn` means Claude decided it was done. The token cap was not reached.
distractor_explanations.D: A prompt line is a weaker fix than removing the structure that teaches Claude to expect more user input and end its turn.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A service detects refusals by testing whether `resp.stop_details.category` is truthy. Normal answers now crash with an `AttributeError` on `None`, and a few refusals still get through as empty replies. The model is one of those that return `stop_reason: "refusal"`. Which change is correct?

options.text: Catch the `AttributeError` and treat the failure as a refusal
Test `resp.content` for an empty list and treat every empty reply as a refusal
Branch on `stop_reason == "refusal"` and treat `stop_details` as optional
Switch to checking the HTTP status, which is a 4xx code for refused requests

questions.explanation: A refusal is a normal HTTP 200 response whose `stop_reason` is `refusal`. `stop_details` is `null` for every other stop reason, and even on a refusal its `category` and `explanation` can be `null`, so keying on `category` both crashes and misses cases. Check `stop_reason` first, then read the details if present. Analogy: an airport gate. Whether a traveller was turned away is shown by the gate agent's decision, not by whether a reason slip happens to be attached. Some turn-aways come with no slip at all, and travellers who were not turned away carry none either, so a slip check both fails and misfires.

distractor_explanations.A: That hides real bugs and still misses refusals whose `category` is `null`. A refusal has a defined signal in `stop_reason`.
distractor_explanations.B: Empty content also appears in an empty `end_turn` response, so it would flag non-refusals while content alone gives no category.
distractor_explanations.D: A refusal is a successful HTTP 200 response, so status-code monitoring never sees it.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A chat service bounds request size by sending only the newest 20 entries of its stored history, using `messages = history[-20:]` on every first-party API call. The history includes tool turns. Occasionally the call fails with HTTP 400 `invalid_request_error`, and every failing slice begins with a `user` message made of a `tool_result` block. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Raise the window from 20 to 40 entries so the cut falls inside a pair less often
Retry the failed call with exponential backoff until the API accepts it
Cut on turn boundaries so each `tool_use` and its `tool_result` stay together
Send the call with `stream=True` so the API validates the history incrementally

questions.explanation: Every `tool_result` must sit in the user message directly after the assistant message holding the `tool_use` it answers, and the `tool_use_id` has to match. A blind slice like `history[-20:]` can cut between the two, leaving a result whose call was dropped, which the API rejects with a 400. Trim in whole turns. Analogy: a pair of socks sold only as pairs. If the packer tears the pack so one sock is left alone, the shop cannot use it. Enlarging the box makes the tear rarer but never impossible, and retrying with the same torn pack gets the same refusal.

distractor_explanations.A: A larger window only makes the bad cut rarer. Some slices would still begin with a result whose `tool_use` was dropped.
distractor_explanations.B: A 400 is a terminal client error. The same malformed slice fails identically on every retry.
distractor_explanations.D: Streaming changes how the response is delivered. The history is validated the same way.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)

options.text: Switch to a non-streaming request and give up incremental output to avoid extra events
Ignore `ping` and any other unrecognised event type instead of throwing in `default`
Add a `ping` case but keep throwing on every other event type the code does not list
Treat `ping` as a dropped connection and restart the whole request from the beginning

questions.explanation: Streams can contain any number of `ping` events, and the versioning policy allows new event types to appear, so a client should skip what it does not understand. Throwing in `default` turns harmless events into outages. Analogy: a mail carrier who finds a flyer in the sack. The right move is to set it aside and keep delivering letters, not to stop the route. Whitelisting only `ping` is like setting aside one kind of flyer: the next new kind stops the route again.

distractor_explanations.A: It gives up incremental output for no good reason. Handling unknown events gracefully is the documented approach.
distractor_explanations.C: This fixes today's error, but new event types may be added later, so the handler would break again.
distractor_explanations.D: A `ping` keeps the connection alive between events and signals nothing wrong with the stream.

questions.prompt:
A job runner wraps its calls like this, and 429 responses are logged and re-raised instead of being queued for later:

```python
try:
    msg = client.messages.create(**params)
except anthropic.APIStatusError as e:
    log.error("API error %s", e.status_code)
    raise
except anthropic.RateLimitError as e:
    queue_for_later(params, e)
```

Which change fixes the behaviour?

options.text: Put the `except anthropic.RateLimitError` clause above the `APIStatusError` one
Catch `anthropic.APIConnectionError` first so 429 responses are routed to the queue
Replace `APIStatusError` in the first clause with the broader `anthropic.APIError`
Set `max_retries=0` on the client so 429 responses raise a different class

questions.explanation: `RateLimitError` is a subclass of `APIStatusError`, which is a subclass of `APIError`. Python runs the first `except` clause that matches, so a general class listed first swallows every specific one below it. List specific classes first. Analogy: a mail-sorting wall with a "general delivery" slot above the "apartment 4B" slot. If every letter fits the general slot first, nothing ever reaches 4B. Putting the specific slot first sends 4B mail home. Changing retries does not alter the class of an error that finally surfaces.

distractor_explanations.B: `APIConnectionError` covers failures to reach the API. A 429 arrives as an HTTP response and never raises it.
distractor_explanations.C: `APIError` is an even more general parent class, so it would still catch the 429 before the specific clause is reached.
distractor_explanations.D: Retries change how often a call is attempted, not which exception class is raised.

questions.prompt:
A gateway wants to throttle itself using the remaining input-token budget reported on each successful first-party call. Its first attempt fails:

```python
msg = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=512, messages=msgs)
left = int(msg.headers["anthropic-ratelimit-input-tokens-remaining"])
```

It raises an `AttributeError`. The gateway must not make a second request to get the value. What is the correct approach?

options.text: Call `messages.with_raw_response.create(...)`, read `.headers`, then call `.parse()`
Read `msg._request_id` and look up the remaining budget by that identifier
Call `client.messages.count_tokens(...)` before each request and subtract the result
Read `msg.usage`, which reports the tokens the account has left this minute

questions.explanation: Parsed SDK response objects do not carry HTTP headers. The `with_raw_response` accessor returns the raw response, so headers such as `anthropic-ratelimit-input-tokens-remaining` are readable, and `.parse()` gives back the same `Message` that `create()` would have returned. Analogy: a parcel and its delivery label. The SDK normally hands you only the parcel's contents, and asking for the raw response gives you the parcel with the label still on it. A tracking number is only an identifier, and a receipt of what you used does not show what is left.

distractor_explanations.B: `_request_id` identifies one call for support. It does not map to any rate-limit data.
distractor_explanations.C: Counting tokens measures one request's size and adds a second call. It cannot show the account's remaining capacity.
distractor_explanations.D: `usage` reports what this one call consumed, not the remaining capacity.

questions.prompt: A nightly job on the first-party API usually sends about 40 requests a minute. After a launch it jumps to 3,000 a minute within seconds. Many calls return 429 `rate_limit_error` with no `enforced_spend_limit_reached` code, yet the Console shows usage below every published RPM and token limit. Cost is acceptable. What is the best fix?

options.text: Move half of the traffic to a model with a larger published RPM
Add a `cache_control` breakpoint so cached tokens stop counting toward ITPM
Raise the organization's monthly spend cap so the 429 responses stop
Ramp the job's traffic up gradually and hold a steady request rate

questions.explanation: Besides the published RPM, ITPM and OTPM limits, the API can return 429 when an organization's usage rises sharply. The documented remedy is to ramp traffic up gradually and keep usage consistent. Analogy: a highway on-ramp with a metering light. The road can carry plenty of cars per hour, but releasing a whole parking lot of cars at the same second jams the merge. Spreading departures over a few minutes gets everyone through. Raising a spend cap is like widening the parking lot, and it does nothing for the merge.

distractor_explanations.A: A different model has its own limits, but the sudden jump in usage would be the trigger there too.
distractor_explanations.B: Usage is already below the ITPM limit. The 429s come from the abrupt change in volume, not from token totals.
distractor_explanations.C: A spend-cap 429 carries the `enforced_spend_limit_reached` code and blocks until month end. These responses do not.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: Since this morning every call from a service returns HTTP 402 with error type `billing_error`, after the account's payment card expired. The retry layer backs off and retries up to ten times on any status other than 400. What is the correct handling?

options.text: Treat it as terminal, stop retrying, and alert whoever owns the account
Rotate the API key and resend the request with the new credential
Keep retrying with longer backoff until the payment issue clears itself
Read the `retry-after` header and pause calls for that many seconds

questions.explanation: A 402 `billing_error` means there is a problem with billing or payment information on the account. It is a configuration problem that a person must fix in the Console, so it should not be retried. Failing fast and alerting the owner restores service sooner than any backoff schedule. The retry layer should list it with other terminal errors.

distractor_explanations.B: A revoked or invalid key returns 401 `authentication_error`. A 402 points at billing or payment information.
distractor_explanations.C: A billing problem will not clear on its own. Retries only add load and delay the alert.
distractor_explanations.D: `retry-after` is sent with ordinary rate-limit 429s. A billing error is not a wait-and-retry condition.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A team hits ITPM 429s on `claude-sonnet-4-5` on the first-party API. It adds `claude-sonnet-4-6` as an overflow route, expecting to double its throughput. The 429s continue with the same volume of traffic overall. Which statement explains this?

options.text: Sonnet 4.6 and 4.5 share one combined limit, so the overflow route adds no headroom
The second model's limit applies after the workspace is configured for it
Limits reset on a fixed minute boundary, so the new route helps only after the next reset
Overflow traffic is counted against both models, doubling the tokens charged to each

questions.explanation: Rate limits are applied per model class, and some classes pool several versions. The published tables state that Sonnet 4.6 and 4.5 share a combined limit, while newer Sonnet versions have separate ones. Splitting traffic between pooled versions therefore adds nothing. Analogy: two phones on one family data plan. Using the second phone does not give the family a second allowance, whereas a separate plan with its own allowance does. The fixed-reset idea is wrong because the allowance refills steadily, like a tap, not once per hour.

distractor_explanations.B: Limits come from the organization's tier and model class, with no per-model workspace step.
distractor_explanations.C: The API uses a token bucket that refills continuously, not a fixed-interval reset.
distractor_explanations.D: Each request is counted once, against the limit of the model that serves it.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A support chat on the first-party API stores each customer line as its own `user` message. A customer sends two lines while Claude is still replying, so the next request ends with an assistant message followed by two consecutive `user` messages. The developer fears a 400 for broken role alternation. What happens?

options.text: Only the final `user` message is kept and the earlier line is silently dropped
The request fails with 400 `invalid_request_error` until the lines are merged client-side
The second line is queued and answered in a separate response after the first
The API combines the consecutive `user` turns into one user turn and answers it

questions.explanation: The Messages API documents that consecutive `user` or `assistant` turns in a request are combined into a single turn, so two back-to-back user messages do not break alternation. The model sees both lines together and writes one reply. Merging on the client is still fine, but it is not required. The request is not rejected, and no line is lost.

distractor_explanations.A: Nothing is dropped. Both messages become content of the single combined turn.
distractor_explanations.B: Consecutive same-role turns are accepted. The API merges them itself.
distractor_explanations.C: The API has no queueing of turns. One request produces one reply to the combined turn.

questions.prompt:
A gateway written without an SDK sends this request to the first-party API. It fails, though the key and model are valid:

```
curl https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages \
  -H "x-api-key: $ANTHROPIC_API_KEY" \
  -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "'"$MODEL"'", "max_tokens": 256,
       "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "ping"}]}'
```

The official SDKs add one more required header automatically, and this call lacks it. Which header is it?

options.text: `anthropic-version`, set to an API version string such as `2023-06-01`
`anthropic-workspace-id`, naming the workspace the call should run in
`anthropic-beta`, listing the beta features enabled for the account
`anthropic-organization-id`, naming the organization that owns the key

questions.explanation: Raw HTTP calls to the Claude API need the credentials, the `content-type: application/json` header, and an `anthropic-version` header. The SDKs send all of these for you, which is why the same call works there. `anthropic-beta` is only for opting in to beta features, and `anthropic-workspace-id` matters only for multi-workspace keys.

distractor_explanations.B: It is required only with a multi-workspace key. A key made for one workspace runs there without it.
distractor_explanations.C: It opts in to beta features only and is not needed for a plain Messages call.
distractor_explanations.D: That name appears as a response header that the API sends back, not as something the caller sets.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A summarizer on the first-party API sets `max_tokens=8000`, although its answers average about 400 tokens. At peak it receives 429 responses that name the output-tokens-per-minute limit. An engineer proposes lowering `max_tokens` to 1000 so each call reserves less output capacity. Truncation is not a concern today. What should the team expect from this change?

options.text: Relief only for streamed calls, where output is metered while it is generated
Large relief, with each call reserving its full `max_tokens` against OTPM when it starts
No relief for OTPM, which counts only the tokens actually generated, not the `max_tokens` ceiling
Input-token headroom instead, with `max_tokens` added to the ITPM estimate

questions.explanation: OTPM is evaluated in real time as tokens are generated and counts only what the model actually produced. The `max_tokens` value is a ceiling and does not factor into OTPM at all, so lowering it from 8000 to 1000 changes nothing for answers that average 400 tokens. Real relief comes from generating fewer tokens or from a higher limit. A lower ceiling only adds a risk of truncation.

distractor_explanations.A: Streamed and non-streamed calls are metered the same way, and neither counts the unused part of the cap.
distractor_explanations.B: Reserving up front is closer to how ITPM is estimated. OTPM is measured as output tokens are produced, so the ceiling is never charged.
distractor_explanations.D: ITPM counts uncached input tokens and cache-creation tokens. The output cap is not part of it.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A Python enricher keeps the SDK's default retries. During a long rate-limit episode the retries run out and `anthropic.RateLimitError` propagates. The job queue wants to re-enqueue the task no sooner than the API says is safe. Where does the code find that wait?

options.text: The `retry-after` header, read from `e.response.headers` when it was sent
In `e.__cause__`, the underlying transport exception raised by the HTTP client
In a duration parsed out of the error body's `message` text with a regex
In `e.status_code`, which holds the number of seconds to wait

questions.explanation: The SDK retries 429s twice by default, honouring `retry-after`, and then raises `RateLimitError`. The exception exposes the HTTP response, so the header is available through `e.response.headers`. It may be missing, as on a spend-cap 429, so read it defensively. Analogy: a clinic receptionist who says "come back at three." That instruction is written on the appointment slip you are handed, not hidden in the receptionist's sigh or the room number. The status code only says that the clinic is busy.

distractor_explanations.B: That attribute is shown for connection failures, which carry no rate-limit information.
distractor_explanations.C: Message wording is not a stable contract. The header is the documented place for the wait.
distractor_explanations.D: `status_code` is the HTTP status, here 429. It is not a duration.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A Python service uses the official SDK with default settings, and its handlers are keyed on exception classes. Which TWO statements about how failures surface are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A client-side `timeout` expiring raises `APITimeoutError`, which has no HTTP status
An HTTP 529 `overloaded_error` raises `InternalServerError` with `status_code` 529
An HTTP 401 `authentication_error` surfaces as `PermissionDeniedError`
An HTTP 529 `overloaded_error` surfaces as `RateLimitError`, so one handler covers 429 and 529
An HTTP 413 `request_too_large` is retried twice by default, like a 5xx error

questions.explanation: The Python SDK maps statuses to classes: 429 is `RateLimitError`, 401 is `AuthenticationError`, 403 is `PermissionDeniedError`, and anything at or above 500, including 529, is `InternalServerError`. A timeout set on the client raises `APITimeoutError`, which comes from the transport and has no response status. Analogy: a post office with separate return stamps. Each stamp is for one reason, and "no answer" has no status stamp at all. Retrying a 413 would not help, since the parcel stays too big.

distractor_explanations.C: `PermissionDeniedError` is the 403 class. A 401 raises `AuthenticationError`.
distractor_explanations.D: `RateLimitError` is the 429 class only. Every status of 500 or above, 529 included, maps to `InternalServerError`.
distractor_explanations.E: The SDK retries connection errors, 408, 409, 429 and 5xx. A 413 is a terminal client error.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A team tunes a client-side throttle for the first-party API, which enforces limits with a token bucket. It reads the `anthropic-ratelimit-*` response headers on every call. Which TWO statements about the limits and headers are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Capacity is replenished continuously up to the maximum, and a short burst can still draw a 429
The combined `anthropic-ratelimit-tokens-*` headers show the most restrictive limit now in effect
The `anthropic-ratelimit-requests-reset` value is a number of seconds to wait before the next call
Message Batches requests count against the same input-token limit as live Messages calls
Each limit resets to full at the top of the minute, so a throttle may spend a whole budget early

questions.explanation: The API refills capacity steadily up to the maximum, so enforcement can happen over short intervals, and a 60 per minute limit may be applied as about one per second. The combined `anthropic-ratelimit-tokens-*` headers show whichever limit is currently the tightest, such as a workspace limit. Analogy: a bathtub with a tap and a drain. The tub refills at a steady rate rather than being emptied and refilled on the hour, and a sudden bucketful can overflow it. The requests-reset value is a clock time, not a countdown, and the batch tub is a different tub.

distractor_explanations.C: The `-reset` headers carry an RFC 3339 timestamp. The wait in seconds comes from `retry-after`.
distractor_explanations.D: The Batches API has its own request limits, shared across models and separate from the Messages limits.
distractor_explanations.E: A token bucket refills continuously, not at fixed boundaries, so a burst can be refused before the minute ends.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A team is choosing between the Python SDK's two ways to stream, `client.messages.create(..., stream=True)` and the `client.messages.stream(...)` context manager. Which TWO statements about them are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: `get_final_message()` returns only the concatenated text of the response, as a string
`create(..., stream=True)` yields raw events and builds no final message object
`text_stream` on the context manager yields only the response's text deltas
Using `client.messages.stream(...)` also requires passing `stream=True` to the call
`stream.text_stream` also yields the partial JSON fragments of `tool_use` inputs

questions.explanation: The `messages.stream()` context manager is the helper style: it exposes `text_stream` for text deltas only and `get_final_message()` for the complete accumulated `Message`. Plain `create(..., stream=True)` returns an iterable of raw events and uses less memory because it builds no final message. Analogy: live subtitles versus a finished transcript. The subtitle feed shows only spoken words as they come, while the transcript service assembles the whole record at the end. A raw tape recorder keeps events but writes no transcript.

distractor_explanations.A: It returns the complete `Message`, with usage and stop reason. Concatenated text comes from `get_final_text()`.
distractor_explanations.D: The helper is a separate method that streams by itself, with no `stream=True` argument.
distractor_explanations.E: It yields text deltas only. Tool input arrives as separate JSON delta events.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt:
A team moves a high-volume reasoning step from Claude Sonnet 5.5 to `claude-haiku-4-5` and keeps the request below. Every call now fails with a 400 error.

```python
client.messages.create(
    model="claude-haiku-4-5",
    max_tokens=4096,
    thinking={"type": "adaptive"},
    output_config={"effort": "low"},
    messages=messages,
)
```

Which change fixes the request while keeping reasoning on?

options.text: Keep `adaptive` and raise `effort` from `low` to `medium`.
Keep `adaptive` and add the `interleaved-thinking-2025-05-14` beta header.
Use `thinking={"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": 2048}` and drop the `effort` setting.
Set `thinking` to `{"type": "disabled"}` and keep `effort` at `low`.

questions.explanation: Claude Haiku 4.5 is an extended-thinking-only model: reasoning is switched on with `thinking: {"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": N}`, where N is at least 1,024 and below `max_tokens`. Adaptive thinking is rejected there with a 400 error, and the `effort` parameter is not supported on it. Analogy: it is like renting a car that only has a manual gearbox. Asking for the automatic mode (adaptive) just gets the request refused, and the fuel-economy dial (effort) is not installed either, so you choose the gear yourself by setting a token budget. The interleaved-thinking header looks tempting but only matters for reasoning between tool calls, which Haiku 4.5 does not offer, so the error stays.

distractor_explanations.A: Haiku 4.5 does not accept adaptive thinking, and it has no effort levels to tune. The effort value was never the real problem.
distractor_explanations.B: That header only affects reasoning between tool calls in manual mode. Haiku 4.5 ignores it, so the adaptive setting is still rejected.
distractor_explanations.D: This turns reasoning off, which the team wants to keep. Effort still has no effect on Haiku 4.5.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A team runs a reasoning step on `claude-haiku-4-5` with `thinking: {"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": N}` and tools attached. Which TWO statements about this setup are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: `budget_tokens` may exceed `max_tokens` whenever tools are in the request.
The budget is a target, so Claude may stop thinking before using all of it.
The `interleaved-thinking-2025-05-14` header makes it reason between tool calls.
An `effort` level can be added to set how deeply it thinks inside the budget.
`budget_tokens` must be at least 1,024 and lower than `max_tokens`.

questions.explanation: Manual thinking has two firm rules: `budget_tokens` must be at least 1,024 and lower than `max_tokens`, and the budget is a target rather than a cap, so Claude may finish thinking early while `max_tokens` remains the hard ceiling. Haiku 4.5 gets none of the extras. Effort is not supported on it, interleaved thinking is not available (the beta header is accepted but ignored), and the exception that lets a budget exceed `max_tokens` belongs to interleaved thinking only. Analogy: telling a contractor to spend about 5,000 on a job. They may finish for less, but the contract's hard limit is a separate, bigger number. The attractive claim about adding effort fails because that dial does not exist on this model.

distractor_explanations.A: The exception applies to interleaved thinking, which Haiku 4.5 lacks. Without it the budget must stay below `max_tokens`.
distractor_explanations.C: Haiku 4.5 does not support interleaved thinking. The Claude API accepts the header and ignores it.
distractor_explanations.D: Effort is not supported on Haiku 4.5. Among extended-thinking-only models, only Claude Opus 4.5 composes effort with a budget.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt:
A tool-heavy support agent runs on `claude-sonnet-5-5` at `medium` effort. Traces show a long up-front thinking pass before the first tool call, and the team wants that pass gone while tool use stays. This request returns a 400 error.

```json
{"model": "claude-sonnet-5-5", "max_tokens": 4096,
 "thinking": {"type": "disabled"},
 "output_config": {"effort": "medium"}}
```

Which change removes the up-front pass and is accepted by the API?

options.text: Send `thinking` as `{"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": 1024}`.
Send `thinking` as `{"type": "between_tools"}` and keep `effort` at `medium`.
Add `"display": "omitted"` to the thinking configuration.
Send `thinking` as `{"type": "adaptive"}` and lower `effort` to `low`.

questions.explanation: Claude Sonnet 5.5 rejects `thinking: {"type": "disabled"}` with a 400 error. Its lowest setting is `between_tools`, which turns off the up-front thinking pass while still allowing reasoning between tool calls; it works at `high` effort or below. Analogy: a chef who normally reads the whole recipe before touching the stove. `between_tools` says to start cooking right away but glance at the pan between steps, and the plain `disabled` switch is simply not on this stove. Hiding the thinking text with `display: "omitted"` is like asking the chef to stop reading notes aloud: the same reading still happens, and the time is still spent.

distractor_explanations.A: Manual budgets are rejected on Sonnet 5.5 with a 400 error, so this does not remove the pass.
distractor_explanations.C: Display only controls whether thinking text comes back. The model still thinks up front, and the tokens are still billed.
distractor_explanations.D: Low effort makes thinking rarer and shorter, but it does not remove the up-front pass. It is too weak for the stated goal.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: An agent on `claude-sonnet-5-5` uses adaptive thinking and several tools. Product wants Claude to reason about each tool result before it picks the next call. An engineer proposes adding the `interleaved-thinking-2025-05-14` beta header to every request. What is the right call?

options.text: Add the header; adaptive thinking does not reason between calls without it.
Add nothing; adaptive thinking already interleaves between tool calls on its own.
Switch to `thinking: {"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": 8000}` for the whole turn.
Raise `effort` to `max`, the only level at which Claude reasons after tool results.

questions.explanation: With adaptive thinking, interleaved thinking is automatic on every model that supports adaptive thinking, and no beta header is needed. The `interleaved-thinking-2025-05-14` header only matters for manual budget mode on older models, and on current models the API simply ignores it. Whether Claude actually thinks after a given tool result is its own per-request decision, which effort steers but never guarantees.

distractor_explanations.A: The header is for manual `budget_tokens` mode on older models. With adaptive thinking the API ignores it and interleaving is automatic.
distractor_explanations.C: Manual budgets are rejected on Sonnet 5.5 with a 400 error. Adaptive thinking is the mode that interleaves there.
distractor_explanations.D: No effort level guarantees thinking after a tool result. Claude decides per request, and follow-up requests that only process results may skip it.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt:
A hand-written agent loop runs adaptive thinking with tools. It works for days, then one request fails with a 400 error saying thinking blocks cannot be modified. The loop rebuilds each assistant turn like this:

```python
KEEP = ("thinking", "text", "tool_use")

messages.append({
    "role": "assistant",
    "content": [b for b in resp.content if b.type in KEEP],
})
```

Which change is correct?

options.text: Retry the failed request with `thinking` set to `{"type": "disabled"}`.
Append `resp.content` exactly as received, with no per-type filtering.
Set `display` to `"summarized"`, which prevents blocks from being redacted.
Drop every thinking block from the turn before sending the `tool_result` back.

questions.explanation: The sequence of thinking blocks in the latest assistant turn must match what the model generated, and that includes `redacted_thinking` blocks, which are safety-redacted pieces of reasoning. A filter on block type silently drops them, so the next request is rejected. Echoing the content array untouched avoids the whole class of bugs. Analogy: mailing back a numbered, signed contract. The receiving office checks every page, and leaving out the one stamped confidential makes the packet invalid even though all the readable pages are present. Turning thinking off for a retry looks like a cure, but it only throws away the reasoning the turn depends on.

distractor_explanations.A: Switching modes mid-turn silently disables thinking and may strip blocks. It hides the cause and costs reasoning quality.
distractor_explanations.C: Display controls the visible text of ordinary thinking blocks. Safety redaction is separate and still produces `redacted_thinking` blocks.
distractor_explanations.D: Within a tool-use turn the thinking blocks must go back complete and unmodified. Dropping them breaks the reasoning chain.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A long advisory chat on `claude-opus-5-5` keeps a large cached history. Early turns need `high` effort and routine follow-ups need `low`, but changing the top-level `output_config.effort` between requests keeps wiping the cache. The team accepts beta features. What should they do?

options.text: Start a fresh conversation for each effort level and paste in a summary of the history.
Send the `mid-conversation-output-config-2026-07-01` header and add an effort-only `role: "system"` message.
Raise the `ttl` on every breakpoint to `1h` and keep switching the top-level effort.
Set `thinking` to `{"type": "disabled"}` on the routine turns and leave effort alone.

questions.explanation: Per-message effort lets a conversation change effort without touching what came before. With the beta header, you insert a `role: "system"` message with empty content and a new `output_config.effort`; it applies from the next user turn, and the earlier messages are unchanged, so the cached prefix still matches. A top-level change is rendered into the whole prompt and restarts the cache. Analogy: leaving a sticky note on the last page of a binder instead of rewriting the first page. Every earlier page stays exactly as printed, so the photocopier's saved copy of them is still valid. A longer retention period would not help, because the trouble is mismatch rather than expiry.

distractor_explanations.A: This avoids cache misses by discarding the history and its reasoning. It is a heavy workaround for a problem with a direct feature.
distractor_explanations.C: A longer lifetime keeps entries alive, but a changed effort value still produces a different prefix that cannot match.
distractor_explanations.D: Claude Opus 5.5 rejects disabled thinking with a 400 error at every effort level.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A research agent that runs for hours on `claude-opus-5-5` still misses its eval bar on the hardest tasks, even at `max` effort. Latency and spend are acceptable to the business, and the failures are about reasoning depth, not tools or prompts. What is the best next step?

options.text: Move the agent to Claude Sonnet 5.5 and use `max` effort to make up the gap.
Run the same evals on `claude-fable-5-1` starting at its default `high` effort.
Switch to Claude Haiku 4.5 with a very large thinking budget to get more reasoning per dollar.
Add `budget_tokens` of 64,000 to the Opus 5.5 requests for deeper reasoning.

questions.explanation: The model lineup runs from Haiku 4.5 (fastest, lowest price) through Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 to Fable 5.1, which is built for demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work. Anthropic's guidance is to try the next tier up when evals at the highest effort levels still fall short, and to decide on eval results rather than assumption. Analogy: a hospital sends a patient to a specialist only after the general doctor's most thorough workup still leaves the question open. Here the failures are about depth, so the specialist (Fable 5.1) is the right referral, while a lower tier or a manual budget cannot supply capability the model lacks.

distractor_explanations.A: Sonnet sits below Opus in capability. Effort adjusts depth within a model and does not close a capability gap between tiers.
distractor_explanations.C: Haiku is the fastest, cheapest tier, built for volume and speed. A bigger budget does not lift it to frontier capability.
distractor_explanations.D: Manual budgets return a 400 error on Opus 5.5. Reasoning depth there is steered through effort.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A team documents how the `effort` parameter behaves on current models before tuning a mixed workload of chat, coding agents and subagents. Which TWO statements are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: `xhigh` suits long-running agentic and coding work, and `low` suits simple tasks like subagents.
Every current model accepts all five levels, including `xhigh` and `max`.
Passing a model's default level explicitly behaves differently from omitting `effort`.
It shapes text, tool calls and thinking alike, and it works even when thinking is off.
`adaptive` is a valid effort value that lets Claude choose its own level of effort per request.

questions.explanation: Effort applies to every output token, so it steers response text, tool calls and thinking together, and it works whether or not thinking is active. The levels have intended uses: `low` for simple, speed-sensitive work such as subagents, and `xhigh` for long-running agentic and coding tasks. Analogy: effort is the master volume knob on a stereo, turning the whole sound up or down at once, not only the bass. The tempting claim that `adaptive` is an effort value mixes up two controls: adaptive is how thinking is switched on, while effort is the knob that scales how hard Claude works.

distractor_explanations.B: Level support varies. Some models that accept `max` do not accept `xhigh`, and Claude Haiku 4.5 does not support effort at all.
distractor_explanations.C: Setting effort to the model's default produces exactly the same behavior as leaving it out.
distractor_explanations.E: Adaptive is a thinking mode, not an effort level. The valid levels are `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` and `max`.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A chat service streams answers from `claude-opus-5-5` with `display: "omitted"`. The bill shows far more output tokens than the visible answers contain, and finance asks how much of that spend was reasoning. Where does the API report it?

options.text: In the length of the returned `thinking` text, which holds the full reasoning that was billed.
By running the saved answers through the token counting endpoint.
In the length of each thinking block's `signature`, which scales with the reasoning.
In `usage.output_tokens_details.thinking_tokens`, a part of the `output_tokens` total.

questions.explanation: Thinking tokens are billed as output tokens even when the text is omitted, so `output_tokens` is larger than what you can see. The response breaks the total down in `usage.output_tokens_details.thinking_tokens`, which is always at most `output_tokens`; when streaming, it appears on the final `message_delta` event.

distractor_explanations.A: With omitted display the `thinking` field is empty. Even summarized text is a summary, not the full reasoning that was billed.
distractor_explanations.B: Token counting measures input for a request. It cannot reveal how many hidden reasoning tokens a past response used.
distractor_explanations.C: The signature is an opaque value that should not be interpreted or parsed. It is not a billing measure.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A content tool asks one prompt to outline a whitepaper, check the outline against the brief, and then write all 3,000 words. Results vary, and a flawed outline is noticed only after the full draft exists. The steps are the same for every job. What is the best redesign?

options.text: Run the single prompt three times in parallel and publish the draft most runs agree on.
Loop the finished draft through a critique-and-rewrite cycle until the model approves it.
Split it into chained calls, with a programmatic check on the outline before the draft is written.
Use a lead call that invents the subtasks for each whitepaper and hands each one to a worker call.

questions.explanation: Prompt chaining fits tasks that decompose cleanly into fixed subtasks: each call is simpler, and you can add a programmatic gate after any intermediate step to confirm the process is still on track. Here the outline is the natural checkpoint, so a bad one never reaches the costly drafting call. Analogy: a builder who has an inspector approve the foundation plan before the concrete is poured. Fixing a flawed plan on paper is cheap; fixing it after the walls are up is not. A critique loop on the finished draft is like inspecting the house after it is built.

distractor_explanations.A: Voting raises confidence in one judgment. It does not catch a bad outline before the expensive draft is written.
distractor_explanations.B: That repairs problems late and needs clear criteria. The weakness is an unchecked early step in a fixed sequence.
distractor_explanations.D: Orchestrator-workers suits subtasks that cannot be predicted. These steps are fixed and known in advance.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A pipeline reviews pull requests for security flaws. A single review catches most issues but misses different ones on different runs, and the team wants more confidence before merging. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Route small diffs to a smaller model and large diffs to a larger one.
Split each diff into sections and review every section in parallel with the same prompt.
Chain one review per file, passing the earlier findings into each next review.
Run differently prompted reviews of each diff in parallel and flag findings that reach a vote threshold.

questions.explanation: Parallelization has two forms. Sectioning splits a task into independent parts that run side by side, while voting runs the same task several times to get diverse outputs and higher confidence, with a threshold deciding what counts. Missed issues that vary from run to run call for voting. Analogy: getting second opinions from several doctors on the same X-ray, and acting on what enough of them flag. Sectioning would be giving each doctor a different organ to examine, which is faster but does not double-check any one organ. Routing resembles sending the patient to one specialist, which does not add opinions.

distractor_explanations.A: Routing matches inputs to handlers, often for cost. It does not raise confidence on any single diff.
distractor_explanations.B: That is sectioning, which speeds up independent parts. It adds no second opinion on the same code.
distractor_explanations.C: Chaining orders dependent steps. It does not give several independent attempts at the same diff.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A team built a prototype on an agent framework. When replies go wrong, nobody can see the exact prompts and responses sent to the model, and debugging stalls. They want the simplest path to a maintainable product. What does Anthropic's guidance suggest?

options.text: Rebuild the core flow on direct API calls and keep a framework only if its internals are known.
Move to an orchestrator-workers design, giving each worker a shorter and more focused prompt to read.
Switch to a more capable model so there are fewer failures to debug.
Add an evaluator agent that critiques every reply before it is sent.

questions.explanation: Frameworks can speed up early work, but they add layers of abstraction that obscure the underlying prompts and responses, which makes debugging harder. Anthropic suggests starting with direct LLM API calls, since many patterns take only a few lines of code, and using a framework only if you understand what it does underneath.

distractor_explanations.B: That changes the architecture, not visibility. The prompts and responses would still be hidden behind the framework.
distractor_explanations.C: A stronger model does not remove the abstraction layer that hides what was sent. The next failure would be just as opaque.
distractor_explanations.D: This adds another component to an already opaque system. It does not expose the underlying prompts.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A coding agent edits a file and is then asked in plain text, `Did that work?`. It almost always answers yes while the test suite still fails. Which design change fits Anthropic's guidance on how agents should assess progress?

options.text: Ask the same yes-or-no question three times and go with the majority answer.
Raise `effort` to `max` and ask for a more careful self-assessment.
Have it rate its confidence from 1 to 10 and stop the loop once the rating passes 8 out of 10.
Feed back real environment results, such as test output, after each step to judge progress.

questions.explanation: Agents operate in a loop, and at each step they need ground truth from the environment, such as tool results or code execution output, to judge whether they are on track. Test output is real evidence; a spoken "it worked" is not. Analogy: a driver using road signs and the odometer rather than gut feeling about whether the exit has passed. Asking for a confidence score or taking a majority of self-checks only polls the same gut feeling more times, so a failing test suite keeps being missed.

distractor_explanations.A: Voting over one unreliable self-check repeats the same blind spot three times.
distractor_explanations.B: More careful reasoning still cannot see test results the agent was never shown.
distractor_explanations.C: A self-reported number is still the model's own opinion. It carries no new evidence about the code.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A team adds a critique-and-revise loop to an essay tool. The reviewer prompt says only `make this better`, and each revision swings between styles with no measurable gain. What does the evaluator-optimizer pattern's guidance say is missing?

options.text: Several reviewers that vote on whether the essay is good enough.
A lead call that splits each essay into subtasks for worker calls.
Clear criteria that let feedback show measurable improvement.
A router that sends each essay to a reviewer prompt specialized for its topic.

questions.explanation: The evaluator-optimizer pattern works when there are clear evaluation criteria and iterative refinement gives measurable value: a generator drafts, an evaluator critiques against stated criteria, and the draft improves each round. With only "make this better", the evaluator has no target, so revisions drift. Analogy: a coach who tells a runner "go faster" versus one who says "cut two seconds off the second lap". The second kind of feedback can be checked and acted on. Adding voters or a router does not supply the missing yardstick.

distractor_explanations.A: Voting adds opinions, but with no stated criteria they would disagree just as vaguely.
distractor_explanations.B: Orchestrator-workers handles unpredictable subtasks. It does not tell a critic what good looks like.
distractor_explanations.D: Routing helps when inputs fall into distinct categories. The loop's problem is a vague target.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A chatbot's single prompt both answers customers and screens each message for inappropriate content. The screening is flaky and the answers have got worse. Added latency must stay minimal. Which redesign fits?

options.text: Screen first in a chained call, and start the answering call only after the screen returns a verdict.
Run answering and screening as separate parallel calls, releasing the answer when the screen passes.
Add a lead call that decides at runtime whether to screen or to answer.
Run the combined prompt several times and release the answer most runs agree on.

questions.explanation: Sectioning, one form of parallelization, runs independent aspects of a task as separate, focused calls at the same time. Anthropic's example is one instance handling the query while another screens it, which tends to work better than one call doing both. Running the two side by side avoids adding the screen's time to every reply. Analogy: a restaurant where one cook prepares your meal while the host checks your reservation, instead of one person doing both in turn. A chained screen-first design is the host finishing before the cook even starts, so every guest waits longer.

distractor_explanations.A: Sequencing the two adds the screen's full latency to every reply, which the stated constraint rules out.
distractor_explanations.C: The need for both jobs is known in advance. A lead call adds a step and still leaves one job per call unsolved.
distractor_explanations.D: Voting repeats the overloaded prompt. It does not give either job its own focused call.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A claims tool has two parts. Part one receives emails of clearly distinct kinds, such as new claims, status questions and complaints, and each kind needs its own prompt and tools. Part two edits a rules repository, where the files to change depend on each ticket and cannot be listed in advance. Which TWO patterns fit these parts? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Evaluator-optimizer for part one, rewriting each reply until a critic approves.
Voting for part one, with three classifiers per email and a majority deciding which handler to use.
Routing for part one, classifying each email and sending it to a handler built for its kind.
Orchestrator-workers for part two, with a lead call choosing the files and delegating the edits.
Prompt chaining for part two, with the order of file edits written in code.

questions.explanation: Routing fits inputs that fall into distinct categories better handled separately: classify first, then hand off to a prompt and toolset built for that category. Orchestrator-workers fits tasks where you cannot predict the subtasks, because the lead call decides them from the specific input, as in code changes that touch an unknown set of files. Analogy: a hotel front desk sends each guest to the right department (routing), while a general contractor surveys each new house and decides which trades to call (orchestrator-workers). Chaining would be a fixed checklist, which cannot cope with changing file sets.

distractor_explanations.A: That loop refines output quality. It does not separate distinct categories into specialized handlers.
distractor_explanations.B: Voting raises confidence in one answer. It does not give each kind of email its own prompt and tools.
distractor_explanations.E: Chaining needs fixed subtasks known up front. Here the set of files varies with each ticket.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A team is about to release its first autonomous agent, which plans its own steps and calls tools in a loop with real side effects. Which TWO practices match Anthropic's guidance for agents? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Judge each step by the agent's own report, without checking tool results.
Remove human checkpoints; an agent that plans on its own never needs input.
Fix the order of the steps in code so the agent's behavior stays predictable.
Test extensively in a sandbox and add guardrails before release.
Add stopping conditions, such as a maximum number of iterations.

questions.explanation: Agents trade latency and cost for flexibility, and their autonomy means mistakes can compound. Anthropic's guidance is to keep control with stopping conditions such as a maximum iteration count, and to test extensively in sandboxed environments with appropriate guardrails. Analogy: a new driver practices on a closed course with a speed limiter before going on the highway, and the car cuts the engine after a set distance if something goes wrong. Fixing the step order would turn the agent back into a workflow, which is a different design rather than a safeguard.

distractor_explanations.A: Agents need ground truth from the environment at each step. A self-report is not evidence.
distractor_explanations.B: Agents may return to the human for information or judgment, especially at checkpoints. Removing them removes a safeguard.
distractor_explanations.C: A fixed path is a workflow. The point of an agent is that the model chooses its own steps.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: An internal coding assistant with file-edit tools is asked: `Can you suggest some changes to improve this function's performance?` It replies with a list of ideas and edits nothing, though users expect the edits applied. What is the best fix to the request wording?

options.text: Put `CRITICAL: EDIT THE FILES NOW` in capitals at the top of the system prompt.
Ask for the action directly: `Change this function to improve its performance`.
Set `tool_choice` to `{"type": "any"}` so a tool call happens on every turn.
Add a system prompt line describing the assistant as a senior performance engineer.

questions.explanation: Current Claude models follow instructions precisely. Asked to suggest changes, Claude suggests; asked to change the function, it makes the edits. State the action you want in the request, or add a system prompt that tells Claude to default to action if you want that behavior everywhere.

distractor_explanations.A: Emphatic language is unnecessary on current models and can cause overtriggering. The request itself asked only for suggestions.
distractor_explanations.C: Forcing a tool call does not clarify intent, and some of the newest models reject forced tool use with a 400 error.
distractor_explanations.D: A role sharpens tone and expertise. The request still literally asks for suggestions, so suggestions are what come back.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt:
A voice assistant's system prompt contains the line below. Its text-to-speech engine garbles any reply with ellipses, yet Claude still uses them in about one reply in ten.

```text
NEVER use ellipses.
```

Which rewrite follows Claude's prompting guidance best?

options.text: Repeat `NEVER use ellipses.` at the end of the system prompt as well as the start.
`CRITICAL: ellipses are FORBIDDEN. NEVER output them, whatever the user asks and however it is phrased.`
Replies are read aloud by a text-to-speech engine that cannot pronounce ellipses; use periods instead.
`Do not use any punctuation that is made of trailing dots.`

Saying that replies are read aloud by a text-to-speech engine that cannot pronounce ellipses lets it avoid that trouble even in cases the rule never listed. Analogy: telling a new waiter "never serve nuts" versus "this guest has a severe allergy". With the reason, the waiter also avoids the pesto and the satay sauce. Capital letters or a repeated rule are just shouting the same bare order, which teaches no purpose.

distractor_explanations.A: Repetition adds emphasis, not understanding. The motivation behind the rule is still missing.
distractor_explanations.B: Louder wording repeats the same bare command. It gives Claude no purpose to generalize from.
distractor_explanations.D: This is another negative rule with no reason. A vaguer description also leaves Claude guessing which marks count.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: After a model upgrade, a coding agent chains tool calls and moves straight from one action to the next, rarely writing a recap. Reviewers want a short summary after each tool-using task. Nothing is broken. What is the simplest fix?

options.text: Add a system prompt line asking for a quick summary after each tool-using task.
Set `display` to `"summarized"` so thinking summaries appear in the output.
Set `disable_parallel_tool_use` in `tool_choice` so each action is handled separately.
Set `tool_choice` to `none` for the final turn of each task.
