distractor_explanations.B: Summarized display returns a summary of thinking blocks. It is not a user-facing recap of the work performed.
distractor_explanations.C: That limits Claude to one tool call per turn. It says nothing about explaining the work.
distractor_explanations.D: This blocks tool calls on that turn. It does not ask Claude to describe what it did.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A research agent has `read_file` and `grep_repo` tools. Traces show it reading five independent files with one call per turn, which makes runs slow. The team wants independent calls batched without forcing dependent calls to run together. What is the best change?

options.text: Tell it to fill missing parameters with best guesses so calls can go out together.
Set `disable_parallel_tool_use` to `false` in the `tool_choice` field.
Tell it to call each available tool once per turn, gathering broad context up front.
Prompt it to run independent calls in parallel and dependent ones in sequence, without guessing.

questions.explanation: Claude's latest models already run independent tool calls in parallel fairly often, and a short prompt block raises that close to every time: call independent tools together, call dependent tools in sequence, and never use placeholders or guess missing parameters. Analogy: two friends shopping from a list. They split up to grab the items in different aisles at the same moment, but one waits to buy the cake mix until the other confirms which recipe the party is using. The `disable_parallel_tool_use` flag only restricts parallelism, and its default already allows it.

distractor_explanations.A: Guessing parameters causes wrong calls. Dependent calls should wait for earlier results.
distractor_explanations.B: False is already the default, so the request would behave exactly as before. Prompt wording is what steers batching.
distractor_explanations.C: This forces needless calls and adds cost. The goal is batching of calls that are truly independent.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A coding agent's task is `make the failing tests pass`. Reviews show it special-cases test inputs with hard-coded return values, and it quietly works around one test that encodes the wrong rule. Which prompt addition targets this?

options.text: Ask for a general solution for all valid inputs, and for wrong-looking tests to be reported.
List the expected output of each test case in the prompt as a worked example.
Require every test to pass before the task may be marked complete.
Lower `effort` to `low`, which stops the agent from building special cases for every test input.

questions.explanation: Claude can focus so hard on making tests pass that it prefers a quick workaround to a general fix. The prompt should say that tests verify correctness rather than define the solution, ask for an implementation that works for all valid inputs without hard-coded values, and tell Claude to report tests that look wrong. Analogy: a student told "score 100% on the quiz" may memorize the answers, while one told "show you understand the topic, and say if a question is wrong" learns the subject. Demanding every test to pass only raises the pressure to cheat.

distractor_explanations.B: Showing the exact cases makes them easier to special-case. It teaches nothing about solving the underlying problem.
distractor_explanations.C: This increases the pressure to satisfy the tests by any means, which is exactly how the shortcuts appear.
distractor_explanations.D: Lower effort reduces how much work Claude does. It does not change the goal of passing tests at any cost.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A support widget shows plain text, but Claude keeps answering with markdown bullets and bold text despite the system prompt line `Do not use markdown.` Which TWO changes follow Claude's prompting guidance? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Say what to write instead, such as `Reply in smoothly flowing paragraphs of plain prose`.
Set `temperature` to 0 for stable formatting of the replies.
Rewrite the system prompt itself in plain prose, without headings, bold text or bullet lists.
Repeat `DO NOT USE MARKDOWN` in capitals at the top and the bottom of the system prompt, plus once per turn.
Add several sample replies full of bullets, each labeled `bad`.

questions.explanation: Two techniques steer format. First, tell Claude what to do instead of what not to do: "write smoothly flowing prose paragraphs" works better than "do not use markdown". Second, match the prompt's own style to the output you want, since a prompt full of markdown tends to produce markdown. Analogy: telling a child "walk" rather than "don't run", and a teacher who writes notes in the handwriting style she wants copied back. Showing bad examples is like demonstrating running to explain what not to do, and it risks being copied.

distractor_explanations.B: Sampling values do not control markdown, and non-default values return a 400 error on the newest models.
distractor_explanations.D: Repeating a negative instruction louder does not tell Claude what style to produce.
distractor_explanations.E: Examples of the unwanted style show Claude the pattern and can pull outputs toward it.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt:
A developer registers a local stdio MCP server with this command. The server never receives its `--port` flag, and the registration does not behave as intended:

```bash
claude mcp add --transport stdio search-db npx -y @acme/search-mcp --port 8080
```

Which command registers the server correctly?

options.text: `claude mcp add --transport http search-db npx -y @acme/search-mcp --port 8080`
`claude mcp add --transport stdio search-db -- npx -y @acme/search-mcp --port 8080`
`claude mcp add --transport stdio --scope project search-db npx -y @acme/search-mcp --port 8080`
`claude mcp add-json search-db npx -y @acme/search-mcp --port 8080`

questions.explanation: For stdio servers, the `--` separator divides Claude's own options (`--transport`, `--env`, `--scope`) from the command that runs the server; everything after it is passed to the server untouched. Without it, Claude Code tries to read `-y` and `--port` as its own options. Analogy: the address block on an envelope versus the note inside. Everything inside the envelope goes to the recipient unread by the postal clerk, and the line that marks where the address ends is the double dash. Changing the scope only decides which shelf the registration is filed on, not how the line is read.

distractor_explanations.A: The http transport expects a server URL, not a command to launch. The flags would still be parsed by Claude Code.
distractor_explanations.C: Scope chooses where the configuration is stored. It does not stop Claude Code from parsing the server's flags.
distractor_explanations.D: The add-json form takes a name followed by a JSON configuration string, not a command line.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A repository's `.mcp.json` defines an HTTP server named `docs` that points at `https://docs.internal.example/mcp`. A developer's user-scope configuration also defines `docs`, with a different URL and extra headers, and their local scope has no `docs` entry. The developer has approved the project's servers. Which definition does Claude Code use for `docs` in that project?

options.text: Neither entry, and the server is skipped until the duplicate name is resolved.
Only the user entry, which outranks the repository's `.mcp.json` file.
Only the project entry; project scope outranks user scope and fields are not merged.
Both entries, with the user's extra headers merged into the URL taken from the project file.

questions.explanation: When one server name is defined in several places, Claude Code connects to it once, using the whole entry from the highest-precedence source: local scope first, then project, then user. Fields are never merged across scopes. Analogy: when two house-rule sheets cover the same room, the guest follows the one posted nearest the door in full and does not blend sentences from the other sheet. The user entry loses here because project scope ranks above user scope, even though it is the developer's own file.

distractor_explanations.A: Claude Code connects once, using the definition from the highest-precedence source.
distractor_explanations.B: Precedence runs local, then project, then user. A personal user-scope entry does not override the project's.
distractor_explanations.D: The whole entry from the winning scope is used, and fields are not merged across scopes.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A team's MCP server exposes tools, runbook resources and a prompt template. They attach it through the `mcp_servers` and `mcp_toolset` fields of a Messages API request. Claude calls the tools, but the runbooks and the template never appear. What is the cause?

options.text: The `mcp_toolset` has no `default_config`, and that block is required before resources can be exposed.
The server uses SSE, and only Streamable HTTP can expose resources.
The connector supports only MCP tool calls; resources and prompts need the app's own MCP client.
Each runbook needs `defer_loading` set to `false` in `configs` before it loads.

questions.explanation: Of the MCP specification, the Messages API connector currently supports tool calls only. Resources and prompts are not exposed through `mcp_servers`, so an app that needs them runs its own MCP client and converts the content with the SDK's MCP helpers. Analogy: a drive-through window that serves only the food menu. The store also sells gift cards and catering trays, but they cannot be ordered at that window, and no setting on the window changes that.

distractor_explanations.A: `default_config` is optional and only sets per-tool defaults. It has no control over resources or prompts.
distractor_explanations.B: The connector accepts both transports. The gap is in which MCP features it supports.
distractor_explanations.D: `defer_loading` governs tool definitions. Resources and prompts are not covered by the connector at all.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A Messages API request attaches a remote server through the MCP connector. The response content holds, in order, a `text` block, an `mcp_tool_use` block and an `mcp_tool_result` block, then more `text`. What should the application do with the `mcp_tool_use` block?

options.text: Run the named tool against the MCP server yourself and reply with a matching `tool_result` block.
Forward the block's `input` to the server over stdio and append the output.
No execution needed; the API already called the server and returned the result next.
Rewrite it into a client `tool_use` block before storing the conversation history.

questions.explanation: With the MCP connector the API acts as the MCP client: it calls the remote server during the request and returns an `mcp_tool_use` block followed by the matching `mcp_tool_result` block. The application has nothing to execute, unlike client tools where it must run the tool and send a `tool_result`. Analogy: ordering through a travel agent who books the flight and hands you both the request slip and the confirmation. You keep the paperwork rather than going to the airline yourself. Treating it like a client tool call would duplicate work that is already done.

distractor_explanations.A: That is the client-tool pattern. With the connector, the call was already made and its result is in the response.
distractor_explanations.B: The connector reaches remote servers over HTTP, and the application has no call left to make.
distractor_explanations.D: Rewriting the block is unnecessary, and the connector's own block types carry the server name and result.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: An agent calls the Messages API with a remote MCP server attached through the connector and passes an OAuth access token in `authorization_token`. Calls work for about an hour and then fail with authorization errors. Who is responsible for fixing this?

options.text: Anthropic's API, which refreshes the token from a stored refresh token.
Nobody; an `mcp_toolset` with `enabled` set to true renews credentials automatically on each request.
The MCP server, which reissues a fresh token on its own with each request.
The application: it must refresh the token and send the new value in `authorization_token`.

questions.explanation: The connector accepts an `authorization_token` but does not run OAuth for you. The application obtains the access token before the call and refreshes it when it expires, then sends the new token on later requests. Analogy: a hotel door reader only checks the key card you hold up. When the card expires at checkout time, the reader cannot print a new one; you must go back to the front desk (your app and the OAuth provider) and get a fresh card. A failure that starts after about an hour points to expiry, and an `enabled` flag on the toolset has no role in credentials.

distractor_explanations.A: The connector only forwards the access token it is given. Handling the OAuth flow and refreshes is left to the caller.
distractor_explanations.B: `enabled` toggles whether tools are available. It has no role in credentials.
distractor_explanations.C: A server validates the token it receives. It does not hand a new one back through the connector.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A team configures an `mcp_toolset` with `default_config` of `{"enabled": false}` and a `configs` entry that sets `search_events` to `{"enabled": true}`. Which TWO statements about how the API treats this request are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: `search_events` is enabled; a `configs` value overrides `default_config`.
One server in `mcp_servers` may be referenced by several toolsets that each carry different rules.
A `configs` key naming a tool the server lacks is not an error; only a warning is logged.
The `default_config` value wins for any tool that also appears in `configs`.
A server listed in `mcp_servers` with no toolset is accepted and exposes all its tools.

questions.explanation: Toolset settings merge with a clear order: a tool's own entry in `configs` beats the set-level `default_config`, which beats the system defaults. So disabling everything by default and enabling one named tool is a valid allowlist. The API also validates the structure: each server needs exactly one toolset, but a tool name in `configs` that the server does not have only triggers a logged warning because servers can change their tools. Analogy: a school rule says "no phones", with a note for one named student allowed to use hers. The named exception wins, and a note naming a student who does not exist is just ignored.

distractor_explanations.B: Each server must be referenced by exactly one MCPToolset. A second toolset for the same server is rejected.
distractor_explanations.D: Precedence runs from tool-specific `configs`, then `default_config`, then system defaults.
distractor_explanations.E: Every server defined in `mcp_servers` must be referenced by a toolset, or validation fails.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt:
A CI job checks out a fork from an unknown contributor and runs the command below. Security wants nothing from the repository's settings files or `.mcp.json` to run on the runner.

```bash
claude -p "List the TODO comments in src/"
```

Which change meets that goal?

options.text: Rely on the workspace trust dialog to block untrusted hooks and MCP servers.
Add a `permissions.deny` rule for `Bash(curl *)` to the runner's settings and run the job as before.
Add `--setting-sources user` so project settings and `.mcp.json` are not read.
Set `"disableAllHooks": true` in the runner's user settings file and leave the rest unchanged.

questions.explanation: A headless `claude -p` run has no trust dialog, so a cloned repository can supply hooks, an `env` block and `.mcp.json` servers that run without any prompt. Passing `--setting-sources user` makes Claude Code read neither the project's settings files nor its `.mcp.json`. Analogy: a night-shift guard who is told to follow only the building owner's rulebook, ignoring any sticky notes a visitor left on the doors. Counting on the usual front-desk check fails because, on this shift, nobody is at the desk. A user-level hook switch is outranked by the visitor's notes.

distractor_explanations.A: A `claude -p` run never shows the trust dialog. Project hooks run, and `.mcp.json` servers connect without asking.
distractor_explanations.B: A deny rule restricts one tool pattern. It does not stop project hooks or MCP servers from loading.
distractor_explanations.D: The repository's project settings take precedence and can set it back to false. It also leaves `.mcp.json` servers untouched.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A team lets Claude drive a browser through the computer use tool to file expense reports. The agent will run unattended on an employee's own laptop, where the browser is already signed in to email and banking. The team wants to limit the damage a hostile web page could do. Which change helps most?

options.text: Run it in a dedicated VM or container with minimal privileges and no signed-in personal accounts.
Rely on the classifiers Anthropic runs on screenshots and keep the laptop setup.
Have Claude sign out of banking at the start of each task and sign in again afterwards.
Add a system prompt line telling Claude to ignore instructions it finds on web pages.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's computer use guidance is to contain the agent: use a dedicated VM or container with minimal privileges, keep sensitive data and login information out of reach, limit internet access to an allowlist of domains, and have a human confirm consequential steps. Built-in classifiers help but are an additional layer. Analogy: letting a contractor work in a workshop with only the tools for the job, not in your living room with your wallet on the table. Telling the contractor to ignore rumors from strangers is nice to have, yet the best protection is that nothing valuable is in reach.

distractor_explanations.B: Those classifiers are an extra layer that steers Claude to double-check instructions. They do not remove access to signed-in accounts.
distractor_explanations.C: Credentials stay within reach of the agent and of any injected instruction. Keeping them out of the environment is safer.
distractor_explanations.D: A prompt instruction is a soft boundary. A hostile page can still steer an agent that has real accounts in reach.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: An agent fetches supplier web pages with a `fetch_page` tool and then acts on them. The team wants a guardrail aimed at hostile instructions hidden in page text, with a verdict the code can branch on. Which design fits?

options.text: Run a harmlessness screen on the user's chat messages before the main call.
Screen each page with a small model returning a boolean, and pass the text on only if it is false.
Ask the main model, in the same call, to rate whether the page is safe before it acts on that page text.
Scan page text with a regex for `ignore previous instructions` and block matches.

questions.explanation: For indirect injection, treat tool output as untrusted and screen it before Claude sees it. Run each result through a lightweight model such as Haiku 4.5 with a JSON-schema output, for example a boolean `injection_suspected`, and return the content as a `tool_result` only if the flag is false; otherwise return an error or a stripped summary. Analogy: a mailroom clerk opens each parcel under a scanner before it reaches the executive's desk. A user-input screen checks the executive's visitors, which is a different door, and a keyword list is a clerk who only knows last year's tricks.

distractor_explanations.A: That guards against a hostile user. Here the user is trusted and the threat sits in the fetched page text.
distractor_explanations.C: The same model reads the hostile text and may be steered by it. Its verdict is also not a separate enforceable check.
distractor_explanations.D: Fixed patterns miss paraphrases and new phrasings. A screening model generalizes better.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A computer use agent books travel for staff. At checkout it meets a cookie banner and a page asking it to accept terms of service before paying. The team wants the agent to run with as little supervision as the tool's safety advice allows. How should these steps be handled?

options.text: Add a system prompt line telling the agent to accept essential cookies and standard terms.
Let the agent click through consent banners and require a human only for the payment.
Raise `effort` to `max` so the agent judges consent screens more carefully.
Pause and ask a human to confirm the terms, the cookies and the payment.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's computer use advice is to ask a human to confirm decisions with meaningful real-world consequences and any task that needs affirmative consent, such as accepting cookies, completing financial transactions, or agreeing to terms of service. The agent can still do the browsing and form-filling unattended and stop at those points. Higher effort or a smarter prompt changes how well the agent reasons, not who has the authority to agree.

distractor_explanations.A: A prompt line leaves the consent decision with the agent. The advice is to have a person make it.
distractor_explanations.B: The guidance puts affirmative-consent tasks such as accepting cookies or terms of service with a human too.
distractor_explanations.C: Deeper reasoning does not change who should decide. Consent and payment steps call for human confirmation.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt:
A 450-line `/repo/CLAUDE.md` is hard to follow, so a developer moves the deploy section into `docs/deploy.md` and replaces it with this line:

```text
Deploy steps: @docs/deploy.md
```

The goal is to keep session context small, and the file sits inside the repo. What happens when a session starts in `/repo`?

options.text: `docs/deploy.md` loads when Claude later reads a file under the `docs/` folder
`docs/deploy.md` stays unloaded until the developer approves it in a one-time dialog
Claude sees only the literal text `@docs/deploy.md` and may open the file with its Read tool
`docs/deploy.md` loads at launch alongside CLAUDE.md; total context is unchanged

questions.explanation: An `@path` import in CLAUDE.md is expanded and loaded into context at launch, alongside the file that names it. Splitting into imports makes the instructions easier to maintain, but it does not shrink what the model reads each session. To load text only when relevant, use path-scoped rules or nested CLAUDE.md files. Analogy: packing one big suitcase versus three smaller bags. You tidied the luggage, yet every bag still boards the plane with you. A bag left at the hotel to collect later is the on-demand loading you did not get here.

distractor_explanations.A: That is how CLAUDE.md files in subdirectories behave. An `@path` import is expanded at launch.
distractor_explanations.B: The approval dialog covers imports that resolve outside the working directory. This path is inside the repo.
distractor_explanations.C: Imports are expanded into context, not left as links for Claude to follow.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A team's LLM judge returns strengths, weaknesses and reasoning before a 1-10 score. On 120 human-labelled support replies its agreement with the humans is 58%. In one pass the team tightens the rubric anchors, adds two scored examples, and swaps in a larger judge model. Agreement rises to 74%, and a reviewer asks which change mattered. What is the best next step?

options.text: Accept the 74% result and start using the judge's scores as the release gate for now
Replace the human labels with the new judge's scores so the set stays consistent
Add a reasoning-before-score step to the judge prompt and measure agreement again
Revert, apply the three changes one at a time, and re-measure on the same 120 cases

questions.explanation: Calibration compares the judge with human-labelled cases and, when agreement is low, fixes the rubric and re-measures. Changing the anchors, the examples and the judge model together tells you the total moved but not why, and a steady total can hide cases that got worse. Move one lever, re-run on the same labelled set, and read the per-case results. Analogy: adjusting a recipe. If you change the salt, the oven temperature and the flour at once, you cannot tell which made the loaf better. The judge's own reasoning is already in place, so adding it again is not the missing piece.

distractor_explanations.A: The number improved, but nobody knows which lever helped or whether a change hurt some cases. The reviewer's question stays open.
distractor_explanations.B: The human labels are the reference being measured against. Using the judge's scores would make the check circular.
distractor_explanations.C: The judge already gives reasoning before its score, so this adds nothing new.
